Discrete Colors

Source: vignettes/articles/r-docs/discrete-color.Rmd
discrete-color.Rmd

Discrete vs Continuous Color

In the same way as the X or Y position of a mark in cartesian coordinates can be used to represent continuous values (i.e. amounts or moments in time) or categories (i.e. labels), color can be used to represent continuous or discrete data. This page is about using color to represent categorical data using discrete colors, but Plotly can also represent continuous values with color.

Discrete Color Concepts

This document explains the following discrete-color-related concepts:

  • color sequences are lists of colors to be mapped onto discrete data values. No interpolation occurs when using color sequences, unlike with continuous color scales, and each color is used as-is. The default color sequence comes from the layout’s colorway attribute and can be explicitly specified using a vector of colors, as in update_layout(colorway = c(...)).
  • legends are visible representations of the mapping between colors and data values. Legend markers also change shape when used with various kinds of traces, such as symbols or lines for scatter-like traces. Legends are configurable under the layout.legend attribute (go_legend()). Legends are the discrete equivalent of continuous color bars

Discrete Color with Plotly

With plotly.core, discrete colors come from mapping a color property (such as a marker’s color) to a factor, character or logical column: the data is split into one trace per category, and each trace gets the next color of the color sequence and its own legend entry. Continuous color comes from passing numeric values to a marker’s color together with a colorscale. This means that numeric strings must be parsed to be used for continuous color, and conversely, numbers used as category codes are best converted to strings.

For example, in the tips dataset, the smoker column is a factor, so its values get discrete colors:

library(plotly.core)
data("tips", package = "reshape2")

tips |>
  go_figure() |>
  add_scatter(
    x = ~total_bill,
    y = ~tip,
    mode = "markers",
    marker = go_scatter_marker(color = ~smoker)
  ) |>
  update_layout(
    title = "String 'smoker' values mean discrete colors",
    legend = go_legend(title = go_legend_title(text = "smoker")),
    plot_bgcolor = "#e5ecf6",
    xaxis = go_xaxis(
      zerolinecolor = "#ffff",
      zerolinewidth = 2,
      gridcolor = "#ffff"
    ),
    yaxis = go_yaxis(
      zerolinecolor = "#ffff",
      zerolinewidth = 2,
      gridcolor = "#ffff"
    )
  )

The size column, however, contains numbers:

library(plotly.core)
data("tips", package = "reshape2")

tips |>
  go_figure() |>
  add_scatter(
    x = ~total_bill,
    y = ~tip,
    mode = "markers",
    marker = go_scatter_marker(
      color = ~size,
      colorscale = "Viridis",
      showscale = TRUE
    )
  ) |>
  update_layout(
    title = "Numeric 'size' values mean continuous color",
    plot_bgcolor = "#e5ecf6",
    xaxis = go_xaxis(
      zerolinecolor = "#ffff",
      zerolinewidth = 2,
      gridcolor = "#ffff"
    ),
    yaxis = go_yaxis(
      zerolinecolor = "#ffff",
      zerolinewidth = 2,
      gridcolor = "#ffff"
    )
  )

Converting this column to strings is very straightforward, and split = ~size then adds one trace per value, but note that the legend lists the values in sorted order, which is the order in which their traces are added (see below for how to control discrete order):

library(plotly.core)
data("tips", package = "reshape2")

tips$size <- as.character(tips$size) #convert to string

tips |>
  go_figure() |>
  add_scatter(
    x = ~total_bill,
    y = ~tip,
    mode = "markers",
    split = ~size
  ) |>
  update_layout(
    title = "String 'size' values mean discrete colors",
    plot_bgcolor = "#e5ecf6",
    xaxis = go_xaxis(
      zerolinecolor = "#ffff",
      zerolinewidth = 2,
      gridcolor = "#ffff"
    ),
    yaxis = go_yaxis(
      zerolinecolor = "#ffff",
      zerolinewidth = 2,
      gridcolor = "#ffff"
    )
  )

Color Sequences in Plotly

By default, Plotly uses the color sequence from the layout’s colorway attribute, which comes from the default plotly template. You can choose any of the following built-in qualitative color sequences however, or define your own.

library("RColorBrewer")
display.brewer.all(type = "qual")

Here is an example that creates a scatter plot using Plotly, with points colored using the qualitative Accent color sequence from RColorBrewer, passed to colorway. Set colorway before adding the traces: the colors are taken from it when the column is mapped.

library(plotly.core)
library(gapminder)
data("gapminder")

gapminder |>
  go_figure() |>
  update_layout(colorway = RColorBrewer::brewer.pal(5, "Accent")) |>
  add_scatter(
    x = ~year,
    y = ~lifeExp,
    mode = "lines",
    line = go_scatter_line(color = ~continent)
  ) |>
  update_layout(
    title = "Built-in Accent color sequence",
    legend = go_legend(title = go_legend_title(text = "continent")),
    plot_bgcolor = "#e5ecf6",
    xaxis = go_xaxis(
      zerolinecolor = "#ffff",
      zerolinewidth = 2,
      gridcolor = "#ffff"
    ),
    yaxis = go_yaxis(
      zerolinecolor = "#ffff",
      zerolinewidth = 2,
      gridcolor = "#ffff"
    )
  )

Explicitly Constructing a Color Sequence

The layout’s colorway attribute accepts explicitly-constructed color sequences as well, as vectors of CSS colors:

library(plotly.core)
library(gapminder)
data("gapminder")

data <- gapminder[gapminder$year == 2007, ]

data |>
  go_figure() |>
  update_layout(colorway = c("red", "green", "blue", "goldenrod", "magenta")) |>
  add_bar(
    x = ~pop,
    y = ~continent,
    width = 1,
    orientation = "h",
    text = ~country,
    hovertemplate = paste(
      "<b>%{text}</b>",
      "<br><b>Continent</b>: %{y}<br>",
      "<i>pop</i>: $%{x}"
    ),
    marker = go_bar_marker(color = ~continent)
  ) |>
  update_layout(
    title = "Explicit color sequence",
    legend = go_legend(title = go_legend_title(text = "continent")),
    plot_bgcolor = "#e5ecf6",
    xaxis = go_xaxis(
      zerolinecolor = "#ffff",
      zerolinewidth = 2,
      gridcolor = "#ffff"
    ),
    yaxis = go_yaxis(
      zerolinecolor = "#ffff",
      zerolinewidth = 2,
      gridcolor = "#ffff"
    )
  )

Warning: If you give colors to fewer traces than the number of unique values in the column you are splitting on, the given colors will be used for some values and the default color sequence for the other values:

library(plotly.core)
data("tips", package = "reshape2")

pal <- c("red", "blue")

fig <- go_figure()
days <- unique(tips$day)
for (k in seq_along(days)) {
  fig <- fig |>
    add_scatter(
      data = tips[tips$day == days[[k]], ],
      x = ~total_bill,
      y = ~tip,
      mode = "markers",
      name = as.character(days[[k]]),
      marker = if (k <= length(pal)) go_scatter_marker(color = pal[[k]])
    )
}
fig <- fig |>
  update_layout(
    title = "Ambiguous! given colors mapped to some values only",
    legend = go_legend(title = go_legend_title(text = "day")),
    plot_bgcolor = "#e5ecf6",
    xaxis = go_xaxis(
      zerolinecolor = "#ffff",
      zerolinewidth = 2,
      gridcolor = "#ffff"
    ),
    yaxis = go_yaxis(
      zerolinecolor = "#ffff",
      zerolinewidth = 2,
      gridcolor = "#ffff"
    )
  )

fig

Directly Mapping Colors to Data Values

The example above assigned colors to data values on a first-come-first-served basis, but you can directly map colors to data values if this is important to your application, by looking up the colors of the column’s levels in a named vector and passing them, in level order, as the colorway. Note that this does not change the order in which values appear in the figure or legend, as can be controlled below:

library(plotly.core)
library(gapminder)
data("gapminder")

pal <- c("red", "green", "blue", "goldenrod", "magenta")
pal <- setNames(pal, c("Europe", "Asia", "Americas", "Oceania", "Africa"))

data |>
  go_figure() |>
  update_layout(colorway = unname(pal[levels(data$continent)])) |>
  add_bar(
    x = ~pop,
    y = ~continent,
    width = 1,
    orientation = "h",
    text = ~country,
    hovertemplate = paste(
      "<b>%{text}</b>",
      "<br><b>Continent</b>: %{y}<br>",
      "<i>pop</i>: $%{x}"
    ),
    marker = go_bar_marker(color = ~continent)
  ) |>
  update_layout(
    title = "Explicit color mapping",
    legend = go_legend(title = go_legend_title(text = "continent")),
    plot_bgcolor = "#e5ecf6",
    xaxis = go_xaxis(
      zerolinecolor = "#ffff",
      zerolinewidth = 2,
      gridcolor = "#ffff"
    ),
    yaxis = go_yaxis(
      zerolinecolor = "#ffff",
      zerolinewidth = 2,
      gridcolor = "#ffff"
    )
  )

If your data set already contains valid CSS colors which you wish to use directly, you can pass them to the marker’s color (e.g. go_bar_marker(color = ...)) of a single trace, in which case there is no legend entry per color, and the color does not appear in the hover label:

library(plotly.core)

go_figure() |>
  add_bar(
    x = c("a", "b", "c"),
    y = c(1, 3, 2),
    marker = go_bar_marker(color = c("red", "goldenrod", "#00D"))
  ) |>
  update_layout(
    plot_bgcolor = "#e5ecf6",
    xaxis = go_xaxis(
      title = "x",
      zerolinecolor = "#ffff",
      zerolinewidth = 2,
      gridcolor = "#ffff"
    ),
    yaxis = go_yaxis(
      title = "y",
      zerolinecolor = "#ffff",
      zerolinewidth = 2,
      gridcolor = "#ffff"
    )
  )

Controlling Discrete Color Order

Plotly lets you specify an ordering over categorical variables with categoryorder, which will apply to axes; the legend follows the order in which traces are added. This can be used with either colorway or explicitly mapped colors.

library(plotly.core)
library(gapminder)
data("gapminder")

data <- gapminder[gapminder$year == 2007, ]

pal <- c("green", "blue", "magenta", "red", "goldenrod")
pal <- setNames(pal, c("Europe", "Asia", "Americas", "Oceania", "Africa"))

data |>
  go_figure() |>
  update_layout(colorway = unname(pal[levels(data$continent)])) |>
  add_bar(
    x = ~pop,
    y = ~continent,
    width = 1,
    orientation = "h",
    text = ~country,
    hovertemplate = paste(
      "<b>%{text}</b>",
      "<br><b>Continent</b>: %{y}<br>",
      "<i>pop</i>: $%{x}"
    ),
    marker = go_bar_marker(color = ~continent)
  ) |>
  update_layout(
    title = "Explicit color sequence with explicit ordering",
    legend = go_legend(title = go_legend_title(text = "continent")),
    plot_bgcolor = "#e5ecf6",
    xaxis = go_xaxis(
      zerolinecolor = "#ffff",
      zerolinewidth = 2,
      gridcolor = "#ffff"
    ),
    yaxis = go_yaxis(
      categoryorder = "array",
      categoryarray = c("Asia", "Oceania", "Europe", "Africa", "Americas"),
      zerolinecolor = "#ffff",
      zerolinewidth = 2,
      gridcolor = "#ffff"
    ),
    bargap = 1
  )
library(plotly.core)
library(gapminder)
data("gapminder")

data <- gapminder[gapminder$year == 2007, ]

pal <- c("red", "green", "blue", "goldenrod", "magenta")
pal <- setNames(pal, c("Europe", "Asia", "Americas", "Oceania", "Africa"))

data |>
  go_figure() |>
  update_layout(colorway = unname(pal[levels(data$continent)])) |>
  add_bar(
    x = ~pop,
    y = ~continent,
    width = 1,
    orientation = "h",
    text = ~country,
    hovertemplate = paste(
      "<b>%{text}</b>",
      "<br><b>Continent</b>: %{y}<br>",
      "<i>pop</i>: $%{x}"
    ),
    marker = go_bar_marker(color = ~continent)
  ) |>
  update_layout(
    title = "Explicit color mapping with explicit ordering",
    legend = go_legend(title = go_legend_title(text = "continent")),
    plot_bgcolor = "#e5ecf6",
    xaxis = go_xaxis(
      zerolinecolor = "#ffff",
      zerolinewidth = 2,
      gridcolor = "#ffff"
    ),
    yaxis = go_yaxis(
      categoryorder = "array",
      categoryarray = c("Asia", "Oceania", "Europe", "Africa", "Americas"),
      zerolinecolor = "#ffff",
      zerolinewidth = 2,
      gridcolor = "#ffff"
    ),
    bargap = 1
  )
